claim: Structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes share conserved structures and serve a common role in maintaining chromosome architecture.
source: Structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes share conserved structures and serve a common role in maintaining chromosome architecture.
evidence: This is a general statement about SMC complexes that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In the bacterium Escherichia coli, the SMC complex MukBEF is necessary for rapid growth and the accurate segregation and positioning of the chromosome.
source: In the bacterium Escherichia coli, the SMC complex MukBEF is necessary for rapid growth and the accurate segregation and positioning of the chromosome, although the specific molecular mechanisms involved are still unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about MukBEF function in E. coli.

claim: The specific molecular mechanisms by which MukBEF controls chromosome segregation and positioning are still unknown.
source: In the bacterium Escherichia coli, the SMC complex MukBEF is necessary for rapid growth and the accurate segregation and positioning of the chromosome, although the specific molecular mechanisms involved are still unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current knowledge about MukBEF mechanisms.

claim: The loading of MukBEF occurs preferentially on newly replicated DNA.
source: Our results indicate that the loading of MukBEF occurs preferentially on newly replicated DNA, at multiple loci on the chromosome where it can promote long-range contacts in cis even though MukBEF can promote long-range contacts in the absence of replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq experiments on synchronized cells presented in the manuscript.

claim: MukBEF loads at multiple loci on the chromosome.
source: Our results indicate that the loading of MukBEF occurs preferentially on newly replicated DNA, at multiple loci on the chromosome where it can promote long-range contacts in cis even though MukBEF can promote long-range contacts in the absence of replication.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data showing long-range contacts appearing at multiple sites upon MukBEF induction.

claim: MukBEF can promote long-range contacts in cis.
source: Our results indicate that the loading of MukBEF occurs preferentially on newly replicated DNA, at multiple loci on the chromosome where it can promote long-range contacts in cis even though MukBEF can promote long-range contacts in the absence of replication.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C experimental data showing long-range DNA contacts.

claim: MukBEF can promote long-range contacts in the absence of replication.
source: Our results indicate that the loading of MukBEF occurs preferentially on newly replicated DNA, at multiple loci on the chromosome where it can promote long-range contacts in cis even though MukBEF can promote long-range contacts in the absence of replication.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C experiments performed on non-replicating cells with MukBEF induction.

claim: The prevention of MukBEF activity increases with the number of matS sites.
source: Using Hi-C and ChIP-seq analyses in strains with rearranged chromosomes, the prevention of MukBEF activity increases with the number of matS sites and this effect likely results from the unloading of MukBEF by MatP.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from strains with varying numbers of matS sites showing graded inhibition of MukBEF activity.

claim: The prevention of MukBEF activity by matS sites likely results from the unloading of MukBEF by MatP.
source: Using Hi-C and ChIP-seq analyses in strains with rearranged chromosomes, the prevention of MukBEF activity increases with the number of matS sites and this effect likely results from the unloading of MukBEF by MatP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between matS sites and reduced MukBEF activity, combined with structural data.

claim: SMC complexes play key roles in many processes involved in chromosome management, from genome maintenance, interphase chromatin organization, sister chromatids alignment, chromosome folding and condensing, to DNA recombination at specific stages of the cell cycle.
source: Structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes play key roles in many processes involved in chromosome management, from genome maintenance, interphase chromatin organization, sister chromatids alignment, chromosome folding and condensing, to DNA recombination at specific stages of the cell cycle (Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A general model for SMC complex activity relies on their properties to bridge DNA elements and by doing so build DNA loops in cis and hold together the sister chromatids in trans.
source: A general model for SMC complex activity relies on their properties to bridge DNA elements and by doing so build DNA loops in cis and hold together the sister chromatids in trans; to do that, they bind DNA and processively extrude a DNA loop in an ATPase-driven loop extrusion, thereby compacting and organizing DNA (Davidson et al., 2019; Ganji et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SMC complexes bind DNA and processively extrude a DNA loop in an ATPase-driven loop extrusion, thereby compacting and organizing DNA.
source: A general model for SMC complex activity relies on their properties to bridge DNA elements and by doing so build DNA loops in cis and hold together the sister chromatids in trans; to do that, they bind DNA and processively extrude a DNA loop in an ATPase-driven loop extrusion, thereby compacting and organizing DNA (Davidson et al., 2019; Ganji et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many molecular features that determine the activity of the various SMC complexes are still unclear.
source: Yet many molecular features that determine the activity of the various SMC complexes are still unclear and it is not known whether they work using the same basal mechanisms (Bürmann et al., 2021; Davidson et al., 2019; Pradhan et al., 2022).
evidence: This acknowledges gaps in current knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: It is not known whether SMC complexes work using the same basal mechanisms.
source: Yet many molecular features that determine the activity of the various SMC complexes are still unclear and it is not known whether they work using the same basal mechanisms (Bürmann et al., 2021; Davidson et al., 2019; Pradhan et al., 2022).
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Smc-ScpAB represents the most highly conserved bacterial SMC complex.
source: In bacteria, Smc-ScpAB represents the most highly conserved complex, while MukBEF and MksBEF represent diverged SMC complexes (Cobbe and Heck, 2004; Yoshinaga and Inagaki, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous comparative studies.

claim: MukBEF and MksBEF represent diverged SMC complexes.
source: In bacteria, Smc-ScpAB represents the most highly conserved complex, while MukBEF and MksBEF represent diverged SMC complexes (Cobbe and Heck, 2004; Yoshinaga and Inagaki, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous comparative studies.

claim: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic SMC complexes are composed of at least five subunits: two Smc subunits, a kleisin subunit, and two additional subunits.
source: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic SMC complexes are composed of at least five subunits: two Smc subunits, a kleisin subunit, and two additional subunits (referred to as kite and hawk subunits, depending on the type of SMC complex).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMC complex composition.

claim: Smc proteins associate with the kleisin protein to form a ring-shaped ATPase assembly.
source: Smc proteins associate with the kleisin protein to form a ring-shaped ATPase assembly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMC complex structure.

claim: The 'Kite' family associates with bacterial and archaeal SMC complexes and also with the eukaryotic SMC5/6 complex.
source: Additional subunits associate with this tripartite complex: the 'Kite' family associates with bacterial and archaeal SMC complexes and also with the eukaryotic SMC5/6 complex while the 'Hawk' family interacts with condensin and cohesin (Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The 'Hawk' family interacts with condensin and cohesin.
source: Additional subunits associate with this tripartite complex: the 'Kite' family associates with bacterial and archaeal SMC complexes and also with the eukaryotic SMC5/6 complex while the 'Hawk' family interacts with condensin and cohesin (Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Additional subunits are thought to be required for SMC activity and to differentiate functions.
source: These additional subunits are thought to be required for the activity and to differentiate functions; for example, while condensin I and II share the same pair of Smc proteins, the difference in the subunit composition specifies their spatiotemporal dynamics and functional contributions to mitotic chromosome assembly (Hirota et al., 2004; Kong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents current understanding in the field.

claim: Condensin I and II share the same pair of Smc proteins, but the difference in the subunit composition specifies their spatiotemporal dynamics and functional contributions to mitotic chromosome assembly.
source: These additional subunits are thought to be required for the activity and to differentiate functions; for example, while condensin I and II share the same pair of Smc proteins, the difference in the subunit composition specifies their spatiotemporal dynamics and functional contributions to mitotic chromosome assembly (Hirota et al., 2004; Kong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, the segregation ParB protein bound to parS site directly binds the Smc subunit.
source: For example, in Bacillus subtilis, the segregation ParB protein bound to parS site directly binds the Smc subunit; the ParB clamp presumably presents DNA to the SMC complex to initiate DNA loop extrusion (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Sullivan et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ParB clamp presumably presents DNA to the SMC complex to initiate DNA loop extrusion in B. subtilis.
source: For example, in Bacillus subtilis, the segregation ParB protein bound to parS site directly binds the Smc subunit; the ParB clamp presumably presents DNA to the SMC complex to initiate DNA loop extrusion (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Sullivan et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a model supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The site-specific recombinase XerD bound to its binding site unloads SMC complexes in the terminus region of the chromosome in B. subtilis.
source: Upon translocation, the site-specific recombinase XerD bound to its binding site unloads SMC complexes in the terminus region of the chromosome and this process is thought to involve specific interactions between the different components (Karaboja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MukBEF was the first SMC complex identified.
source: MukBEF was the first SMC complex identified.
evidence: This is a historical fact in the field.

claim: In Escherichia coli, MukBEF is thought to be required for chromosome segregation as muk mutants present many anucleate cells or mis-segregated chromosomes.
source: In Escherichia coli, MukBEF is thought to be required for chromosome segregation as muk mutants present many anucleate cells or mis-segregated chromosomes (Niki et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MukBEF promotes DNA contacts in the megabase range within each replication arm.
source: MukBEF promotes long-range interactions along the chromosome except in the 800-kb-long terminal domain (Ter) where MatP prevents its activity (Lioy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MukBEF promotes long-range interactions along the chromosome except in the 800-kb-long terminal domain (Ter) where MatP prevents its activity.
source: MukBEF promotes long-range interactions along the chromosome except in the 800-kb-long terminal domain (Ter) where MatP prevents its activity (Lioy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Under conditions of increased chromosome occupancy of MukBEF, the E. coli chromosome appears to be organized as a series of loops around a thin (<130 nm) MukBEF axial core.
source: Under conditions of increased chromosome occupancy of MukBEF, the E. coli chromosome appears to be organized as a series of loops around a thin (<130 nm) MukBEF axial core (Mäkelä and Sherratt, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Whether MukBEF is loaded at a particular locus is still an open question.
source: Whether MukBEF is loaded at a particular locus is still an open question.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The complete atomic structure of MukBEF in complex with MatP and DNA has been determined by electron cryomicroscopy.
source: The complete atomic structure of MukBEF in complex with MatP and DNA has been determined by electron cryomicroscopy (Bürmann et al., 2021); it also contains the MukBEF binding partner AcpP protein (Prince et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The MukBEF complex contains the MukBEF binding partner AcpP protein.
source: The complete atomic structure of MukBEF in complex with MatP and DNA has been determined by electron cryomicroscopy (Bürmann et al., 2021); it also contains the MukBEF binding partner AcpP protein (Prince et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The MukBEF complex binds two distinct DNA double helices reminiscent of the arms of an extruded loop.
source: It revealed that the complex binds two distinct DNA double helices reminiscent of the arms of an extruded loop, MatP-bound DNA threads through the MukBEF ring, while the second DNA is clamped by MukF, MukE, and the MukB ATPase heads.
evidence: This is based on structural data from cryoEM studies.

claim: MatP-bound DNA threads through the MukBEF ring.
source: It revealed that the complex binds two distinct DNA double helices reminiscent of the arms of an extruded loop, MatP-bound DNA threads through the MukBEF ring, while the second DNA is clamped by MukF, MukE, and the MukB ATPase heads.
evidence: This is based on structural data from cryoEM studies.

claim: The second DNA in the MukBEF complex is clamped by MukF, MukE, and the MukB ATPase heads.
source: It revealed that the complex binds two distinct DNA double helices reminiscent of the arms of an extruded loop, MatP-bound DNA threads through the MukBEF ring, while the second DNA is clamped by MukF, MukE, and the MukB ATPase heads.
evidence: This is based on structural data from cryoEM studies.

claim: MatP might be an unloader of MukBEF.
source: The presence of MatP in the complex together with its ability to prevent MukBEF activity prompted authors to propose that MatP might be an unloader of MukBEF (Bürmann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in a previous study, cited here.

claim: Long-range DNA contacts within replication arms, outside Ter, result from MukBEF activity.
source: The rationale was based on previous findings showing that long-range DNA contacts within replication arms, outside Ter, result from MukBEF activity.
evidence: This is based on previous findings mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: If MukBEF loads at a specific locus, long-range contacts should appear and spread from this site upon MukBEF synthesis.
source: If MukBEF loads at a specific locus as observed for Smc-ScpAB at parS sites, we would expect to detect the appearance and spreading of long-range contacts from this site upon MukBEF synthesis.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the experimental design.

claim: If MukBEF loads stochastically or at multiple loci on the chromosome, long-range contacts should occur at multiple sites.
source: By contrast, if MukBEF loads stochastically or at multiple loci on the chromosome, long-range contacts should occur at multiple sites.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the experimental design.

claim: The mukBEF operon was cloned onto a medium-copy number plasmid under control of a pLac promoter and introduced in a mukF mutant to conditionally synthesize MukBEF.
source: To conditionally synthesize MukBEF, the mukBEF operon was cloned onto a medium-copy number plasmid under control of a pLac promoter and introduced in a mukF mutant.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: In the absence of inducer, no growth was detected at 37°C for the mukF mutant carrying the inducible mukBEF plasmid.
source: In the absence of inducer, as observed for a mukF mutant, no growth was detected at 37°C and the amount of anucleated cells at 22°C was similar to that of the mukF mutant (13% vs 15%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The amount of anucleated cells at 22°C for the mukF mutant carrying the inducible mukBEF plasmid without inducer was similar to that of the mukF mutant (13% vs 15%).
source: In the absence of inducer, as observed for a mukF mutant, no growth was detected at 37°C and the amount of anucleated cells at 22°C was similar to that of the mukF mutant (13% vs 15%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Induced expression of mukBEF functionally complemented the absence of MukF, restoring growth at 37°C in Lennox Broth (LB).
source: Induced expression of mukBEF functionally complemented the absence of MukF, restoring growth at 37°C in Lennox Broth (LB) (Figure 1A) and accurately segregating the chromosome at 22°C, as evidenced by the low amount of anucleate cells (<2%) observed in the presence of the inducer (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Induced expression of mukBEF accurately segregated the chromosome at 22°C, as evidenced by the low amount of anucleate cells (<2%) observed in the presence of the inducer.
source: Induced expression of mukBEF functionally complemented the absence of MukF, restoring growth at 37°C in Lennox Broth (LB) (Figure 1A) and accurately segregating the chromosome at 22°C, as evidenced by the low amount of anucleate cells (<2%) observed in the presence of the inducer (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Long-range DNA contacts were hardly visible after 20 min of MukBEF induction.
source: Hi-C contact maps were established 20min, 40min, and 2 hr after induction and compared to that obtained in the absence of induction (Figure 1C with Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C): long-range DNA contacts were hardly visible after 20 min (Figure 1C with Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), were readily observed after 40 min, and reached after 2 hr a level similar to that observed in wild-type (WT) strains (Figure 1 with Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Long-range DNA contacts were readily observed after 40 min of MukBEF induction.
source: Hi-C contact maps were established 20min, 40min, and 2 hr after induction and compared to that obtained in the absence of induction (Figure 1C with Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C): long-range DNA contacts were hardly visible after 20 min (Figure 1C with Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), were readily observed after 40 min, and reached after 2 hr a level similar to that observed in wild-type (WT) strains (Figure 1 with Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Long-range DNA contacts reached after 2 hr of MukBEF induction a level similar to that observed in wild-type (WT) strains.
source: Hi-C contact maps were established 20min, 40min, and 2 hr after induction and compared to that obtained in the absence of induction (Figure 1C with Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C): long-range DNA contacts were hardly visible after 20 min (Figure 1C with Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), were readily observed after 40 min, and reached after 2 hr a level similar to that observed in wild-type (WT) strains (Figure 1 with Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The increase of contacts does not originate from a specific position on the chromosome but rather appears from numerous sites.
source: Altogether, the results indicate that the increase of contacts does not originate from a specific position on the chromosome but rather appears from numerous sites, suggesting that the activity of MukBEF does not initiate at a single locus but rather from multiple loci along the chromosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hi-C data showing contacts appearing at multiple sites.

claim: The activity of MukBEF does not initiate at a single locus but rather from multiple loci along the chromosome.
source: Altogether, the results indicate that the increase of contacts does not originate from a specific position on the chromosome but rather appears from numerous sites, suggesting that the activity of MukBEF does not initiate at a single locus but rather from multiple loci along the chromosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hi-C data showing contacts appearing at multiple sites.

claim: The MatP/matS system has been shown to prevent MukBEF activity in Ter.
source: The MatP/matS system has been shown to prevent MukBEF activity in Ter (Lioy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Long-range DNA interactions were readily observed on both regions flanking Ter2 in strains LiTer9, LiTer7, and LiTer4.
source: Long-range DNA interactions were readily observed on both regions flanking Ter2 in both three strains, and long-range contacts are affected in the Ter2 segment, even when only four matS were present (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Long-range contacts are affected in the Ter2 segment, even when only four matS were present.
source: Long-range DNA interactions were readily observed on both regions flanking Ter2 in both three strains, and long-range contacts are affected in the Ter2 segment, even when only four matS were present (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The 136 kb region carrying four matS sites in LiTer4 was sufficient to decrease long-range contacts promoted by MukBEF activity.
source: Remarkably, the 136 kb region carrying four matS sites in LiTer4 was sufficient to decrease long-range contacts promoted by MukBEF activity.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data comparing LiTer4 to its matP deletion derivative.

claim: The median range of contact for Ter in the WT condition is 263±24 kb.
source: The median range of contact for Ter in the WT condition is 263±24 kb.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Hi-C data.

claim: No significant differences in the range of contacts (275±9 kb) were observed in strain Liter9 for the Ter2 segment carrying nine matS.
source: Remarkably, no significant differences in the range of contacts (275±9 kb) were observed in strain Liter9 for the Ter2 segment carrying nine matS; it is noteworthy that this region carrying nine matS sites shows the same range of contacts (280±35 kb) in the WT configuration.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Hi-C data.

claim: A transposed 253 kb region carrying nine matS prevent MukBEF activity as much as the same segment present in the 838-kb-long Ter MD.
source: This result shows that a transposed 253 kb region carrying nine matS prevent MukBEF activity as much as the same segment present in the 838-kb-long Ter MD.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of range of contacts in different configurations.

claim: For the 209 kb segment carrying seven matS sites, the range of contact was increased to 330±9 kb.
source: For the 209 kb segment carrying seven matS sites, the range of contact was increased to 330±9 kb while it increased to 352±12 kb for the 136 kb segment with four matS.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Hi-C data.

claim: For the 136 kb segment with four matS, the range of contact increased to 352±12 kb.
source: For the 209 kb segment carrying seven matS sites, the range of contact was increased to 330±9 kb while it increased to 352±12 kb for the 136 kb segment with four matS.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Hi-C data.

claim: Segments carrying seven or four matS affect MukBEF activity, even though at a lower level than a 250 kb segment with nine matS sites.
source: These results indicate that segments carrying seven or four matS affect MukBEF activity, even though at a lower level than a 250 kb segment with nine matS sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative comparison of range of contacts.

claim: Three matS sites in a 136 kb segment can prevent MukBEF activity.
source: The ratio of normalized contact maps of the LiTer4 ΔmatS26 or LiTer4 ΔmatS28 strains to the corresponding ΔmatP derivative (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) revealed that long-range contacts were affected by the presence of only three matS sites in the 136 kb segment.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from strains with matS deletions.

claim: The density of three matS sites (matS25-matS26 and matS27) in strain LiTer4 ΔmatS28 seems to be as efficient (range contact of 357±11 kb) as the four matS sites in strain LiTer4 (range contact of 352±12 kb).
source: By measuring the range of contacts in strains LiTer4 ΔmatS26 and LiTer4 ΔmatS28 (Figure 3E), the density of three matS sites (matS25-matS26 and matS27) in strain LiTer4 ΔmatS28 seems to be as efficient (range contact of 357±11 kb) as the four matS sites in strain LiTer4 (range contact of 352±12 kb).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from Hi-C data.

claim: In LiTer4 ΔmatS26, the range of contact is increased to 370±6 kb indicating a reduced ability to prevent MukBEF activity.
source: By contrast, in LiTer4 ΔmatS26, the range of contact is increased to 370±6 kb indicating a reduced ability to prevent MukBEF activity.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from Hi-C data.

claim: The density of matS sites in a small chromosomal region has a greater impact than dispersion of the same number of matS sites over a larger segment.
source: Altogether, assuming that differences in the matS sequences do not modify MatP's ability to bind to the chromosome and affect its capacity to inhibit MukBEF, these results suggested that the density of matS sites in a small chromosomal region has a greater impact than dispersion of the same number of matS sites over a larger segment.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of different matS configurations.

claim: ChIP-seq experiments using a Flag version of MukB on synchronized cells showed a two- to fourfold enrichment in the regions that have been replicated.
source: Normalized ChIP-seq experiments were performed by normalizing the quantity of immunoprecipitated fragments to the input of MukB-Flag. This experiment showed a two- to fourfold enrichment in the regions that have been replicated (Figure 4A with Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: After 10 min of replication restart, the ChIP-seq signal was increased over 500 kb on each side of oriC.
source: After 10 min, the signal was increased over 500 kb on each side of oriC.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 20 min after replication restart, the ChIP-seq signal progressed and corresponded to the regions that have been replicated.
source: At 20 min, the signal progressed and corresponded to the regions that have been replicated.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 40 min after replication restart, when the chromosome has been fully replicated, the signals obtained in the ChIP-seq samples indicated an enrichment of MukBEF all along the chromosome except in a 1.5 Mb region centered on the Ter region.
source: At 40 min, when the chromosome has been fully replicated, the signals obtained in the ChIP-seq samples indicated an enrichment of MukBEF all along the chromosome except in a 1.5 Mb region centered on the Ter region.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MukBEF enrichment drops to basal levels 250 kb before Ter.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, MukBEF enrichment drops to basal levels 250 kb before Ter (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: MukBEF enrichment followed the progression of replication and spread from oriC toward Ter.
source: This enrichment followed the progression of replication and spread from oriC toward Ter.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data at different time points.

claim: MukBEF is loaded into regions newly replicated either at the replication fork or even further behind it, except in the Ter region from which it would be excluded.
source: Altogether, these findings indicate that MukBEF is loaded into regions newly replicated either at the replication fork or even further behind it, except in the Ter region from which it would be excluded.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing enrichment following replication.

claim: In the LiTer7 strain, MukBEF is preferentially associated with newly replicated sequences and shows a twofold increase following replication fork progression.
source: As in the WT background, MukBEF is preferentially associated with newly replicated sequences and shows a twofold increase following replication fork progression.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A break in the MukBEF enrichment profile is detected in the sequence corresponding to Ter2 in the LiTer7 strain.
source: However, a break in this enrichment profile is detected in the sequence corresponding to Ter2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MukBEF does not bind or persist in segments carrying matS sites.
source: These results suggest that MukBEF does not bind or persist in segments carrying matS sites, and that the MatP/matS system prevent residence of MukBEF in that region.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing reduced enrichment in Ter2.

claim: The MatP/matS system prevent residence of MukBEF in regions carrying matS sites.
source: These results suggest that MukBEF does not bind or persist in segments carrying matS sites, and that the MatP/matS system prevent residence of MukBEF in that region.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing reduced enrichment in Ter2.

claim: In the absence of replication and of MukBEF, long-range contacts were constrained by barriers that delimit domains, called chromosome-interacting domains (CIDs).
source: In the absence of replication and of MukBEF, long-range contacts were constrained by barriers that delimit domains, called chromosome-interacting domains (CIDs) (Figure 4C with Figure 4—figure supplement 2), previously detected in WT cells in growing conditions (Lioy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: After 2 hr of MukBEF induction in non-replicating cells, long-range contacts were detected except in the Ter region.
source: Remarkably, after 2 hr of MukBEF induction in non-replicating cells, long-range contacts were detected except in the Ter region, indicating that MukBEF activity does not require newly replicated DNA to promote long-range contacts (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: MukBEF activity does not require newly replicated DNA to promote long-range contacts.
source: Remarkably, after 2 hr of MukBEF induction in non-replicating cells, long-range contacts were detected except in the Ter region, indicating that MukBEF activity does not require newly replicated DNA to promote long-range contacts (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from Hi-C data showing long-range contacts in non-replicating cells with MukBEF.

claim: Restarting replication for 40 min after 2 hr of MukBEF induction did not alter significantly the range and distribution of long-range DNA contacts observed in the absence of replication but in the presence of MukBEF outside Ter.
source: Finally, restarting replication for 40 min after 2 hr of MukBEF induction did not alter significantly the range and distribution of long-range DNA contacts observed in the absence of replication but in the presence of MukBEF outside Ter.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data comparing replicating and non-replicating conditions.

claim: Replication does not appear to be an essential process for the activity of MukBEF.
source: As previously observed by microscopy in E. coli, replication does not appear to be an essential process for the activity of this SMC complex (Badrinarayanan et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and a citation to previous work.

claim: MukBEF promotes long-range DNA contacts independently of the replication process even though it binds preferentially in newly replicated regions.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that MukBEF promotes long-range DNA contacts independently of the replication process even though it binds preferentially in newly replicated regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP-seq and Hi-C data.

claim: In E. coli, there are 28 matS sequences dispersed throughout the 1.03 Mb Ter domain.
source: In E. coli, there are 28 matS sequences dispersed throughout the 1.03 Mb Ter domain.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq analysis identifying matS sites.

claim: The average matS density is three matS per 100 kb.
source: The average matS density is three matS per 100 kb, but this distribution is not uniform and the matS density doubles in the vicinity of the dif sequence (Figure 5 with Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the matS distribution analysis.

claim: Only nine matS are sufficient to completely inhibit MukBEF activity.
source: Despite the fact that only nine matS are sufficient to completely inhibit MukBEF activity, matS sites have been selected and consequently a large portion of the E. coli chromosome is inaccessible to MukBEF.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that nine matS sites prevent MukBEF activity as effectively as the full Ter.

claim: matS sites have been selected and consequently a large portion of the E. coli chromosome is inaccessible to MukBEF.
source: Despite the fact that only nine matS are sufficient to completely inhibit MukBEF activity, matS sites have been selected and consequently a large portion of the E. coli chromosome is inaccessible to MukBEF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary conservation of matS sites.

claim: The Ter domain was defined as the longest stretch of matS sequences between areas that are at least 100 kb devoid of matS.
source: The Ter domain was defined as the longest stretch of matS sequences between areas that are at least 100 kb devoid of matS.
evidence: This describes the method used for comparative genomics analysis.

claim: The size of the Ter domain varies from 300 kb to 1 Mb, representing 6–25% of the chromosome, and contains 6–77 matS.
source: The size of the Ter domain varies from 300 kb to 1 Mb, representing 6–25% of the chromosome, and contains 6–77 matS (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data shown in Table 1.

claim: In most of these species, more than 14 matS sequences are distributed over 540 kb.
source: In most of these species, more than 14 matS sequences are distributed over 540 kb, and the Ter domain always contains the dif sequence.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data shown in Table 1.

claim: The Ter domain always contains the dif sequence.
source: In most of these species, more than 14 matS sequences are distributed over 540 kb, and the Ter domain always contains the dif sequence.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data shown in Table 1.

claim: The number of matS per kb increases for all species and reaches its maximum near the dif site.
source: As shown in Figure 5, the number of matS per kb increases for all species and reaches its maximum near the dif site.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MukBEF loading does not only involve the Ori region but also different regions of the chromosome.
source: By different ChIP-seq and Hi-C approaches performed in different strains, some of which have undergone programmed genetic rearrangements, we showed that MukBEF loading does not only involve the Ori region but also different regions of the chromosome.
evidence: This is supported by the combined ChIP-seq and Hi-C data from various strains.

claim: MukBEF molecules are bound to the chromosome, molecules are removed or displaced by replication, MukBEF molecules readily reassociate in newly replicated regions except in Ter region in which the unloading of MukBEF is enhanced by MatP bound to matS sites.
source: These results support a model in which MukBEF molecules are bound to the chromosome, molecules are removed or displaced by replication, MukBEF molecules readily reassociate in newly replicated regions except in Ter region in which the unloading of MukBEF is enhanced by MatP bound to matS sites.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the combined experimental data.

claim: MukBEF may organize a series of loops around a thin MukBEF axial core.
source: Our results are in agreement with the previous proposal that MukBEF may organize a series of loops around a thin MukBEF axial core (Mäkelä and Sherratt, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and a citation to previous work.

claim: The activity of MukBEF appears to be more similar to that of eukaryotic condensins than to that of the Smc-ScpAB complex.
source: Thus, the activity of MukBEF appears to be more similar to that of eukaryotic condensins than to that of the Smc-ScpAB complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of MukBEF activity with other SMC complexes.

claim: In the absence of parB, Smc-ScpAB is still able to perform chromosome segregation almost perfectly.
source: Remarkably, in the absence of parB, Smc-ScpAB is still able to perform chromosome segregation almost perfectly (Ireton et al., 1994; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MukBEF inhibition is graded with the number of matS.
source: By varying the number of matS sites at an ectopic position, we showed that MukBEF inhibition is graded with the number of matS; while an effect is already visible with three matS scattered over a 78 kb region, the maximal effect seems to be reached with nine matS sites distributed over a 253 kb region.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from strains with varying numbers of matS sites.

claim: An effect on MukBEF activity is already visible with three matS scattered over a 78 kb region.
source: By varying the number of matS sites at an ectopic position, we showed that MukBEF inhibition is graded with the number of matS; while an effect is already visible with three matS scattered over a 78 kb region, the maximal effect seems to be reached with nine matS sites distributed over a 253 kb region.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from strains with varying numbers of matS sites.

claim: The maximal effect of MukBEF inhibition seems to be reached with nine matS sites distributed over a 253 kb region.
source: By varying the number of matS sites at an ectopic position, we showed that MukBEF inhibition is graded with the number of matS; while an effect is already visible with three matS scattered over a 78 kb region, the maximal effect seems to be reached with nine matS sites distributed over a 253 kb region.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from strains with varying numbers of matS sites.

claim: The density of matS sites seems to affect the inhibition efficiency.
source: Accordingly, the density of matS sites seems to affect the inhibition efficiency supporting this assumption.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of different matS configurations.

claim: The structure of the MukBEF-AcpP-MatP/matS complex obtained by cryoEM revealed the entrapment of two topologically separated DNA segments in two distinct compartments called 'ring' and 'clamp'.
source: The structure of the MukBEF-AcpP-MatP/matS complex obtained by cryoEM revealed the entrapment of two topologically separated DNA segments in two distinct compartments called 'ring' and 'clamp', with the matS site present in the ring compartment.
evidence: This is based on structural data from a previous study.

claim: The matS site is present in the ring compartment of the MukBEF-AcpP-MatP/matS complex.
source: The structure of the MukBEF-AcpP-MatP/matS complex obtained by cryoEM revealed the entrapment of two topologically separated DNA segments in two distinct compartments called 'ring' and 'clamp', with the matS site present in the ring compartment.
evidence: This is based on structural data from a previous study.

claim: One of the MatP monomers forms a contact with one of the MukE monomers while the joint binds and positions MatP between the MukB arms.
source: One of the MatP monomers forms a contact with one of the MukE monomers while the joint binds and positions MatP between the MukB arms.
evidence: This is based on structural data from a previous study.

claim: The joint interface is much larger than the MukE-MatP bridge and likely provides the major binding energy for association.
source: The joint interface is much larger than the MukE-MatP bridge and likely provides the major binding energy for association (Bürmann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on structural data from a previous study.

claim: A change to alanine of the five residues between H38 and D42 in contact with MukE did not affect MatP's ability to inhibit MukBEF activity.
source: Indeed, a change to alanine of the five residues between H38 and D42 in contact with MukE did not affect MatP's ability to inhibit MukBEF activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from the MatP5A mutant shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: MukBEF activity is detected by the appearance of contacts over a distance of approximately 1 Mb, spanning around 4 Mb of the chromosome (excluding the Ter domain).
source: MukBEF activity is detected by the appearance of contacts over a distance of approximately 1 Mb, spanning around 4 Mb of the chromosome (excluding the Ter domain).
evidence: This is a summary of the Hi-C data observations.

claim: MukBEF molecules can be discharged from DNA in the absence of MatP, i.e., outside Ter.
source: Even if the molecular details of this activity remain to be characterized, it is tempting to speculate that MukBEF molecules can be discharged from DNA in the absence of MatP, i.e., outside Ter.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that MukBEF activity is limited to ~1 Mb contacts.

claim: MukBEF activity does not appear to be significantly disrupted in a matP mutant.
source: Furthermore, it can be noted that MukBEF activity does not appear to be significantly disrupted in a matP mutant, suggesting that MukBEF can be discharged from DNA in the absence of MatP.
evidence: This is inferred from Hi-C data comparing wild-type and matP mutant strains.

claim: MatP is not the MukBEF unloader per se, but rather its ability to prevent MukBEF activity has been selected to protect the Ter region from a condensin activity.
source: Altogether, the results would indicate that MatP is not the MukBEF unloader per se, but rather that its ability to prevent MukBEF activity has been selected to protect the Ter region from a condensin activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined experimental data and evolutionary considerations.

claim: MatP confers another property to Ter, through an interaction of its C-terminus with the septum-associated protein ZapB and localizing Ter at midcell.
source: MatP has already been shown to confer another property to Ter, through an interaction of its C-terminus with the septum-associated protein ZapB and localizing Ter at midcell.
evidence: This is based on previous knowledge about MatP function.

claim: Inhibiting MukBEF does not require MatP's anchoring of Ter at the septum of division.
source: Remarkably, these two properties are independent as inhibiting MukBEF does not require its anchoring of Ter at the septum of division (Lioy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MukBEF presence is mostly banished from the dif region.
source: Given that the number of matS sites far exceeds the number required to prevent MukBEF activity and that the density of matS sites increases as we approach dif, we may speculate that MukBEF presence is mostly banished from the dif region.
evidence: This is speculation based on the matS distribution data.

claim: Resolution of chromosome dimers by XerC-XerD recombinases occurs in the dif region.
source: At least two activities of DNA metabolism occur in this region: resolution of chromosome dimers by XerC-XerD recombinases and the post-replicative decatenation of circular chromosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA metabolism at dif.

claim: Post-replicative decatenation of circular chromosomes occurs in the dif region.
source: At least two activities of DNA metabolism occur in this region: resolution of chromosome dimers by XerC-XerD recombinases and the post-replicative decatenation of circular chromosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA metabolism at dif.

claim: MukBEF could interfere with TopIV activity and delay potential chromosome decatenation.
source: We may speculate, based on in vitro observations (Kumar et al., 2022), that MukBEF could interfere with TopIV activity and delay potential chromosome decatenation.
evidence: This is speculation based on in vitro observations cited.

claim: Chromosome dimers resolved at the dif site may become trapped in loops formed by MukBEF, thus delaying segregation.
source: Another possibility is that chromosome dimers resolved at the dif site may become trapped in loops formed by MukBEF, thus delaying segregation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential MukBEF interference with chromosome dimer resolution.

claim: In the absence of replication and of MukBEF activity, the contact map displayed a single strong diagonal composed of very well-defined CIDs, ranging in size from 20 to 400 kb.
source: In the absence of replication and of MukBEF activity, the contact map displayed a single strong diagonal composed of very well-defined CIDs, ranging in size from 20 to 400 kb.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from non-replicating cells without MukBEF.

claim: The CIDs, clearly visible in populations of cells growing exponentially, were prominent in non-replicating conditions without MukBEF revealing the impact of transcription on the structuring of the genome.
source: The CIDs, clearly visible in populations of cells growing exponentially, were prominent in these conditions revealing the impact of transcription on the structuring of the genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hi-C data showing prominent CIDs in specific conditions.

claim: Upon replication, the CID organization is less apparent because of the new contacts that occur between loci belonging to different CIDs.
source: Upon replication, the CID organization is less apparent because of the new contacts that occur between loci belonging to different CIDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hi-C data comparing replicating and non-replicating conditions.

claim: The induction of MukBEF in the presence of replication further attenuates the patterning of CIDs.
source: The induction of MukBEF in the presence of replication further attenuates the patterning of CIDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hi-C data with MukBEF induction.

claim: Transcription, replication, and condensin activity each contribute to the organization of bacterial genomes.
source: Altogether, these results highlight the respective contribution of these three processes, transcription, replication, and condensin activity, on the organization of bacterial genomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined Hi-C data under different conditions.

claim: All E. coli strains used in this study are derived from E. coli MG1655.
source: All E. coli strains used in this study are derived from E. coli MG1655.
evidence: This describes the experimental materials used.

claim: Three independent ChIP-seq experiments revealed 28 matS and a newly derived consensus sequence.
source: To clarify this, three independent ChIP-seq experiments were performed, revealing 28 matS and a newly derived consensus sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MukBEF can operate to form long-range contacts between two Ter segments.
source: These results indicated that MukBEF can operate to form long-range contacts between the two Ter segments and that MatP can prevent MukBEF activity when segments carrying matS sites are moved in different locations of the genome.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from the RiTer11 strain.

claim: MatP can prevent MukBEF activity when segments carrying matS sites are moved in different locations of the genome.
source: These results indicated that MukBEF can operate to form long-range contacts between the two Ter segments and that MatP can prevent MukBEF activity when segments carrying matS sites are moved in different locations of the genome.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from strains with transposed Ter segments.

claim: MukBEF activity can be initiated from multiple regions of the chromosome, in the right, left, or Ori regions.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that MukBEF activity can be initiated from multiple regions of the chromosome, in the right, left, or Ori regions, and that Ter segments cannot insulate DNA segments devoid of matS sites.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from strains with transposed segments.

claim: Ter segments cannot insulate DNA segments devoid of matS sites.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that MukBEF activity can be initiated from multiple regions of the chromosome, in the right, left, or Ori regions, and that Ter segments cannot insulate DNA segments devoid of matS sites.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data showing long-range contacts between Ter segments.

claim: MukBEF does not globally translocate from the Ori region to the terminus of the chromosome as observed with Smc-ScpAB in different bacteria.
source: They also reveal that MukBEF does not globally translocate from the Ori region to the terminus of the chromosome as observed with Smc-ScpAB in different bacteria.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hi-C data showing contacts appearing at multiple sites rather than spreading from Ori.

claim: Ter segments carrying 17 and 11 matS can prevent MukBEF activity and restrict DNA contacts.
source: Furthermore, the results indicated that Ter segments carrying 17 and 11 matS can prevent MukBEF activity and restrict DNA contacts.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data from the RiTer11 strain.
